title: When Words Take on New Meanings
summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about the hosts' new studio and welcome Will and Man Guesh of Part Time Genius, who discuss their podcast, their move from Mental Floss, and guests such as a water sommelier and Daniel Pink on the science of timing. The episode then turns to words with changed or misused meanings: decimate, hedonism and epicurean (from Epicurus), cynic and cynicism (Diogenes, Rousseau), cakewalk (its plantation and minstrel-show origins), piece of cake, Kafkaesque, luddite (the Ned Ludd weavers and class struggle, and C.P. Snow's 1959 usage), and nimrod (the biblical Nimrod, Tower of Babel, and Bugs Bunny). The episode closes with listener mail from Peter in Vancouver criticizing the earlier vaping episode, to which the hosts respond, and the sign-off.

segments.title: Opening banter and Part Time Genius guests
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about their new studio, then welcome Will and Man Guesh of Part Time Genius, discussing their podcast schedule, their history at Mental Floss, and interesting guests they have had.

segments.title: Descriptivists, prescriptivists, and decimate
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the episode on words whose meanings have changed, contrasting descriptivist and prescriptivist views, and discuss the word decimate, which has shifted from reducing by ten percent to meaning widespread destruction.

segments.title: Hedonism and Epicurean
segments.summary: The hosts explain that hedonism originally was a Greek philosophy about maximizing pleasure and minimizing pain, not mainly about debauchery, citing Jeremy Bentham's philosophic calculus. They then discuss epicurean, from the philosopher Epicurus, who emphasized moderation and inner tranquility.

segments.title: Cynic and cynicism
segments.summary: The hosts describe the modern meaning of cynicism as distrust, contrast it with the ancient Greek Cynics who rejected comforts, and recount Diogenes of Sinope. They note that the modern usage is often traced to Rousseau's critique of the Enlightenment.

segments.title: Ancient Greece aside and transition to cakewalk
segments.summary: A brief tangent on the appeal of ancient Greece, then a transition to the nineteenth century.

segments.title: Cakewalk origins
segments.summary: The hosts explain that the cakewalk was a plantation contest in the antebellum South where enslaved people imitated white society for a cake prize, that minstrel shows later distorted it, and that the modern sense of an easy task comes from this. They also discuss the Saturnalia comparison and the origin of piece of cake.

segments.title: Kafkaesque
segments.summary: The hosts describe Franz Kafka's recurring themes of struggle against faceless bureaucracy and how Kafkaesque came to describe absurd bureaucracy, and they note it is often misused for minor bad luck. They quote Frederick Karl's definition.

segments.title: Luddite
segments.summary: The hosts explain that the modern sense of luddite as technophobe differs from the original early nineteenth-century Luddites, who were textile workers protesting automated looms as a class struggle, named after Ned Ludd. They note C.P. Snow's 1959 usage and the 1970 New Scientist use.

segments.title: Nimrod
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the biblical Nimrod, founder of Babylon credited with the Tower of Babel, the origin of different languages, and how Bugs Bunny's use of nimrod for Elmer Fudd popularized the insult, with some 1980s slang usage.

segments.title: Listener mail on vaping episode
segments.summary: Peter from Vancouver writes that the earlier vaping episode mocked vapers and overlooked harm reduction and quitting smoking. The hosts respond that they did research and apologize for the excessive mockery, while noting that tobacco is worse.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts give contact information and social media handles and sign off.
